summary: Supply the CFO, the interest expense, the fixed capital investment and the free cash flow to firm and the Free cash flow to firm (FCFF) calculator solves for net income. It is built for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Free cash flow to firm (FCFF) calculator work?
sections.html:
The Free cash flow to firm (FCFF) calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports net income in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (select source); then you type in the CFO, the interest expense, the fixed capital investment and the free cash flow to firm (FCFF).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Free cash flow to firm (FCFF) calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Net income=-depreciation and amortization + free cash flow to firm (FCFF) + fixed capital investment + interest expense × corporate tax rate − interest expense + working capital investment
EBITDA=(depreciation and amortization × corporate tax rate − free cash flow to firm (FCFF) − fixed capital investment − working capital investment) ÷ (corporate tax rate − 1)
EBIT=(depreciation and amortization − free cash flow to firm (FCFF) − fixed capital investment − working capital investment) ÷ (corporate tax rate − 1)
Corporate tax rate=(CFO − free cash flow to firm (FCFF) − fixed capital investment + interest expense) ÷ interest expense
EBITDA=(depreciation and amortization × corporate tax rate − depreciation and amortization + interest expense × corporate tax rate − interest expense − net income) ÷ (corporate tax rate − 1)
Depreciation and amortization=-EBIT + EBITDA

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Free cash flow to firm (FCFF) calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the CFO, the interest expense and the fixed capital investment — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Free cash flow to firm (FCFF) calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns net income, derived from the CFO, the interest expense and the fixed capital investment. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Free cash flow to firm (FCFF) calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the CFO, the interest expense, the fixed capital investment and the free cash flow to firm, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter net income in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Net income opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Free cash flow to firm (FCFF) calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
